issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s requirement for possession for own use must be genuine and honest, and objectively amount to a need that the court considers reasonable.
material_facts: The landlords sought possession for their own use, saying that their existing accommodation was insufficient for their family’s needs.
The landlords’ family members lived together, and the existing accommodation consisted of several rooms in the building.
Accommodation said to be available to one landlord was subject to the owner’s claim to recover possession, while proceedings to recover the father’s accommodation were also pending.
The High Court considered subsequent changes in the family, including additional marriages and a child, and found no basis to conclude that the accommodation was sufficient.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the landlords had a bona fide requirement was a finding of fact supported by the circumstances, and the eviction order was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under the East Punjab Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, the statutory requirement that the landlord requires the premises for own use protects tenants from eviction based merely on contractual rights. A landlord’s honest desire for possession must have the objective element of a genuine need, and the court must consider whether gratifying that need is reasonable in light of all relevant circumstances, so that tenant protection is not rendered illusory. A conclusion inferred from primary facts, including a conclusion about bona fide requirement, may be a question of fact rather than law.

rule.if: landlord_use_eviction_case and landlord_family_shares_accommodation and existing_accommodation_insufficient and (other_claimed_accommodation_not_secure or family_needs_expanded)

predicates.landlord_use_eviction_case: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the premises were required for the landlord’s own use.
predicates.landlord_family_shares_accommodation: The landlord’s family members lived together and relied on shared accommodation.
predicates.existing_accommodation_insufficient: The court found that the accommodation already available to the landlord’s household did not meet its needs.
predicates.other_claimed_accommodation_not_secure: Other accommodation said to be available to members of the household was subject to claims or proceedings for recovery of possession.
predicates.family_needs_expanded: The court considered later changes in the household that increased or affected its accommodation needs.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession for own use, the household shares accommodation that is insufficient, and other claimed accommodation is insecure or household needs have expanded, the rule treats the eviction order as upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may reappraise evidence when the governing revisional power permits review of legality and propriety and the appellate finding is infirm in law.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the High Court’s reappraisal of the Appellate Authority’s factual findings in revision.
The revisional power authorized the High Court to satisfy itself as to the legality and propriety of the order under revision.
The High Court considered that the Appellate Authority had relied on material that was not relevant to the landlords’ need and had otherwise reached an infirm finding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled, in an appropriate case, to reappraise the evidence and interfere with the appellate finding; its exercise of revisional jurisdiction was not barred merely because the finding concerned facts.
issues.legal_principle: The extent of revisional jurisdiction depends on the language of the provision conferring it. Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, permits review of the legality and propriety of the order, a wider formulation than review only of whether an order is according to law. Revisional review is not a second first appeal, but in an appropriate case it permits examination of factual findings that are infirm in law. The Court relied on Bell & Co. Ltd. v. Waman Hemraj, Hari Shankar v. Girdhari Lal Chowdhury, Dattonpant Gopalvarao Devakate v. Vithalrao Marutirao, and M/s Ranalakshmi Dyeing Works v. Rangaswamy; it distinguished Mattulal v. Radhe Lal and Phiroze Bamanji Desai v. Chandrakant M. Patel as addressing different limits on second appeals or narrower revisional powers.

predicates.rent_eviction_revision: A court reviewed an appellate order in a revision arising from a rent-eviction proceeding.
predicates.revision_standard_covers_legality_and_pr: The governing revisional power authorizes scrutiny of whether the order is legal and proper.
predicates.appellate_finding_legally_infirm: The appellate finding rested on irrelevant material or was otherwise infirm in law.

issues.definition: In a rent-eviction revision, when the review power covers legality and propriety and the appellate finding is infirm in law, the revisional court may reappraise the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Courts may cautiously consider subsequent events when moulding relief, and a later acquisition by one claimant does not defeat an eviction claim supported by the continuing accommodation needs of other co-owners.
material_facts: The High Court took account of family changes occurring after the eviction proceeding began, including later marriages and the birth of a child.
The tenant later asserted that one landlord’s wife had acquired another residential building.
The Court held that, even taking account of that acquisition, the needs of the other co-owners supported the eviction order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court properly considered subsequent events cautiously, and the later acquisition asserted by the tenant did not undermine the eviction order because the needs of the other co-owners independently supported it.
issues.legal_principle: Courts may take cautious cognizance of subsequent events to mould relief. The effect of a later event depends on the circumstances; here, the asserted acquisition did not defeat the relief because the accommodation needs of the other co-owners remained sufficient to support the order.

predicates.landlord_need_eviction_case: A landlord sought eviction on the basis of a need for accommodation.
predicates.subsequent_event_occurred: A relevant change occurred after the eviction proceeding began, including a change in family circumstances or an asserted acquisition of other housing.
predicates.remaining_coowners_independently_need_ac: The court found that co-owners other than the person associated with the later acquisition still had accommodation needs supporting the claim.

issues.definition: When a relevant event occurs after a landlord-need eviction proceeding begins but the remaining co-owners still independently need accommodation, the eviction order remains supportable.
